newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO defence heads to debate command structure.
newsitem.headline: NATO defence heads to debate command structure.

text.p: NATO's military chiefs meet in Brussels on Tuesday to try and agree radical changes to the alliance's command structure designed to bring it into line with the realities of the post-Cold War world.

The Chiefs of Defence Staffs (CHODs) from the 16 NATO allies will review a number of proposals making the huge military machine created to defeat the Soviet Union in a war that never took place leaner and fitter.

As well as saving money, the reforms will equip the alliance to undertake more Bosnia-style peacekeeping missions and allow it to expand eastwards into former communist Europe without becoming overly bureaucratic and unwieldy.
"The reforms are critical if a new NATO is to truly evolve," said one military source.
The defence chiefs will examine proposals to create two strategic commands, one for the Atlantic zone based in the U.S, and one for the European zone based in northern Europe.
A current central command, based in Britain, formerly responsible for protecting the approaches to the North Sea from Russia, would be scrapped.
Under these commands there would be a slimmed-down network of regional commands, responsible for such things as the southern and northern European flanks.
Then, there would be a final layer of sub-regional commands with more specific duties, such as one in Portugal protecting the Atlantic approaches to the Mediterranean.
If adopted, the package would result in the scrapping of an entire command level and several headquarters, and remove the danger of command proliferation as the alliance takes in more members.
"Instead of 65 headquarters at four levels of command, we would have 25 at three levels," said one senior NATO military source.

Without the reforms, NATO would find it impossibly expensive to absorb new members, such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, as planned and build close military ties with partnership countries from central and eastern Europe.

The package of measures also seeks to give the European allies a greater say in the U.S.-dominated Atlantic alliance and creates a mechanism whereby Europeans could take more responsibility for security affairs on their own continent.

NATO was created in 1949 to defend the Western allies from attack by the Soviet Union and its command structure reflected a defensive posture no longer in tune with the likely security demands of the 21st century.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), the organisation which gives practical expression to the transatlantic links, sees reforms as establishing it as the main security organisation of the post-Cold War world.

Given the spiralling costs of defence and tightening budgets, the Europeans are keen to develop a European security identity within NATO rather than create new defence organisations outside the alliance.
France has linked the development of a real European voice to its full reintegration into the military wing of the alliance it quit in 1966 in a row over U.S. dominance.

Paris is pushing for the key AfSouth Mediterranean command to be given to a European instead of an American commander -- a demand rejected by Washington which is instead pushing a compromise of a European deputy followed by a full review in five years time.
The package of measures also foresees the creation of a deputy European commander to the U.S.' Supreme Allied Commander in Europe who would take overall charge of any European operation.

The defence chiefs will not try and solve that problem, but hope to find broad agreement on the new command structure and the creation of Combined Joint Task Forces (CJTFs) which would allow small groups of NATO to take on "out of theatre" missions.

The CJTF concept, which would also provide the basis of any European-only operation, has been boosted by an agreement to allow the Western European Union, the EU's designated defence arm, to use NATO facilities for such operations.

Under a complicated deal reached last week, non-EU NATO countries Turkey and Norway would take part in the planning and running of such operations, once approved by NATO's policy-making body of the ambassadors of the 16 members.
